summary: Gogoro CEO Horace Luke is making India the company's next major market, with the first commercial launch of its battery-swapping network and smartscooters in December 2023. The Taiwanese company is using Taiwan as the template, with 30 Delhi stations planned by Q1 2024 and multibillion-dollar investment plans, while its Taiwan revenue and profit have fallen. The article also covers India's small EV market, the stalled Hero MotoCorp partnership, and the need for battery-swapping standardization.
one_line: Gogoro is betting on India's huge two-wheeler market as a launch pad for global growth, replicating its Taiwan battery-swapping model despite weakening Taiwan results.
key_facts: Gogoro co-founder and CEO Horace Luke wants to "go big" in India, the world's biggest two-wheeler market, where 15 million to 20 million new two-wheelers hit the road every year.

Gogoro was founded in 2011 by former HTC executives Horace Luke and Matt Taylor, and calls itself the Android of all EVs; it licenses its technology to other manufacturers and sells its own scooters with swappable batteries.
Gogoro already operates in China, Indonesia, Singapore, Israel and the Philippines, plus Taiwan, and sees India as a launch pad starting with neighboring Nepal.
Earlier India moves include a Delhi battery-swapping pilot, a partnership with Belrise Industries to invest a total of $2.5 billion in Maharashtra, and a $25 million investment in Zypp Electric.
Gogoro assembles components in Maharashtra in partnership with Foxconn and is working with domestic manufacturers to localize production.
About 11 vehicle manufacturers in Taiwan, including Suzuki, Yamaha and Aeon Motor, build vehicles on Gogoro's standard battery size, and some may come to India over time.
Gogoro partnered with Hero MotoCorp in April 2021 to roll out battery swapping in India, but the deal has not yielded results; Luke says Hero is B2C-focused while Gogoro is launching B2B first.
Gogoro plans 30 stations in Delhi by Q1 2024; in Taiwan it grew from 30 stations in Taipei to 12,500 stations serving about 600,000 vehicles.
Luke said Pan-India investment could be "several billion dollars easily by 2030–2032."
Gogoro's system captures 93% of electric vehicles in Taiwan, about 80% of which use its own branded vehicles.

In its latest quarter, revenue fell 10.2% year-on-year to $91.8 million, with a net loss of $3.1 million versus net income of $56.4 million a year earlier; battery-swapping revenue rose 10.4% to $33.6 million.
Luke blamed Taiwan's decline on lobbying against EV adoption speed after the 2020 elections and a slow post-COVID-19 recovery.
EVs are only 3.7% of India's automotive market, and electric scooters are about 90% of EV sales but only about 5% of the two-wheeler market; the government targets 30% EV adoption by 2030.
A Bain & Company and Blume Ventures report says batteryless electric two-wheelers can cut upfront cost by 40% to 50% but that building a swapping ecosystem will be challenging near term.
